project.name: poker-champ
project.description: A real-time multiplayer Texas Hold'em poker platform built as a monorepo with a Node.js/Colyseus/Express backend, an Expo/React Native frontend, shared Zod contract packages, and Prisma for PostgreSQL persistence.

nodes.name: .claudeignore
nodes.summary: Claude AI ignore file listing patterns that should be excluded from AI-assisted code analysis, such as build artifacts, lock files, and generated output directories.

nodes.name: .env.example
nodes.summary: Root-level environment variable template documenting required server-side configuration including PORT, Stripe payment keys, feature flags for pay-gating and membership purchase, and pricing constants.

nodes.name: .fallowrc.json
nodes.summary: Fallow dead-code analysis configuration defining monorepo entry points, workspace packages, ignore patterns for tests and generated files, dependency and export ignore lists, duplicate detection, custom rules, and health thresholds.
nodes.languageNotes: Fallow is a Rust-based dead export/import scanner; this config drives its monorepo-aware analysis of the poker-champ workspace.

nodes.name: client-build-smoke.yml

nodes.name: contract-first.yml
nodes.summary: GitHub Actions workflow enforcing OpenAPI-first discipline by verifying that openapi.json is updated alongside openapi.ts changes, requiring a BREAKING marker on version bumps, and confirming SDK types stay in sync via pnpm sdk:gen.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses bash inline scripting to diff OpenAPI versions across git SHAs, enforcing contract-first discipline at the CI layer.

nodes.name: headless-harness.yml
nodes.summary: GitHub Actions workflow triggered on engine, rooms, state, and lobby changes that runs the headless two-client multiplayer integration harness to catch real-time synchronization regressions.

nodes.name: lessons-canonical-ci.yml

nodes.name: server-phase4-soak-gate-nightly.yml
nodes.summary: Nightly GitHub Actions workflow running extended Phase7 validation and PokerRoom soak tests with 85-minute timeouts, uploading structured log artifacts and running canary gate analysis on hand completion rates.

nodes.name: server-phase4-soak-gate.yml
nodes.summary: GitHub Actions workflow triggered on engine and room changes that runs a quick Phase7 validation and PokerRoom soak gate with 30-minute timeout and canary hand-completion rate checks.

nodes.name: server-rejoin-regression.yml
nodes.summary: GitHub Actions workflow running the multiplayer churn matrix and server rejoin regression tests on changes to the engine, rooms, state, or test directories.

tour.title: Project Overview & Monorepo Structure
tour.description: The server entry point at apps/server/src/index.ts is the best single file to understand what this project is and how its pieces connect. It bootstraps the Colyseus WebSocket game server, registers all Express HTTP routers, wires the TournamentDirector tick, and starts background reconciliation jobs. Reading it gives you an immediate map of every major subsystem: game rooms, REST API, tournaments, economy, and auth all converge here in one startup sequence.
tour.languageLesson: This is a TypeScript monorepo (apps/server, apps/client, packages/*). The server uses the Colyseus framework for stateful WebSocket rooms alongside a conventional Express REST API — both run in the same process. The `turbo.json` build graph ensures packages are compiled before apps.

tour.title: The Realtime Contract
tour.description: Before looking at either client or server in depth, the realtime-contract package (packages/realtime-contract/src/index.ts) defines the shared language they speak. It is a pure Zod-schema package — no runtime logic — that exports every WebSocket message shape: player actions, lobby events, table snapshots, and error codes. Both client and server import from here, so any change to message structure is a compile-time error on both sides.
tour.languageLesson: Zod schemas serve as a single source of truth for runtime validation and static TypeScript types simultaneously. Using `z.infer<typeof Schema>` means the type and the validator can never diverge — if the server sends a field the client's schema doesn't know about, Zod strips or rejects it at parse time.

tour.title: Persistence Layer: Prisma Schema & DB Package
tour.description: The Prisma schema (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma) defines 28+ models covering every durable entity: PokerTable, Hand, HandAction, HandPayout, User, Tournament, Leaderboard, and more. The @poker-champ/db package (packages/db/src/index.ts) wraps a singleton PrismaClient that every server consumer imports. With 66 fan-in references it is the single most depended-upon module in the entire codebase, making it foundational to understand early.
tour.languageLesson: Prisma uses a single schema.prisma file as the canonical source for both the database DDL and the generated TypeScript client. The `prisma migrate` workflow creates incremental SQL migration files in packages/db/prisma/migrations/, keeping schema evolution auditable and reversible.

tour.title: The PokerRoom: WebSocket Session Container
tour.description: PokerRoom (apps/server/src/rooms/PokerRoom.ts) is the Colyseus room class that each connected poker table instantiates. It is the outer container: it owns the WebSocket lifecycle (onCreate, onJoin, onLeave, onDispose), delegates every concern to a PokerRoomController, and mediates between the network layer and the Dealer engine beneath it. Understanding PokerRoom's shape — what it owns vs. what it delegates — is the key to navigating the entire server-side call graph.
tour.languageLesson: Colyseus rooms use a Schema-based state sync model: every property annotated with @type() on the root Schema class is automatically delta-encoded and broadcast to all connected clients on every state mutation. This means server code can mutate state freely without manually tracking what to push — the framework handles diffing.

tour.title: Replicated Game State: PokerState
tour.description: PokerState (apps/server/src/state/PokerState.ts) is the Colyseus Schema class that holds everything the client needs to render a table: table config, blind structure, board cards, current street, and the ArraySchema of player seats. Because Colyseus auto-syncs this to every client on mutation, PokerState acts as the single source of truth for both server logic and client rendering — there is no separate REST endpoint for live game data.
tour.languageLesson: Colyseus Schema classes use decorator-based reflection (@type, @MapSchema, @ArraySchema). Only annotated properties participate in state sync; plain class fields remain server-private. This lets the PokerState class hold both the public replicated surface and private server-only runtime fields side by side.

tour.title: The Dealer Engine: Hand Lifecycle
tour.description: The Dealer (apps/server/src/engine/Dealer.ts) is the top-level game engine facade that PokerRoom holds. Internally it is decomposed into focused services: HandOrchestrator coordinates the sequence of waiting → dealing → street advancement → showdown, HandLifecycleService contains the pure card-game logic, and TurnManager provides a serialised action queue that ensures concurrent client messages never corrupt hand state. This layered decomposition keeps each service unit-testable in isolation.
tour.languageLesson: The TurnManager's ActionQueue is a serialised promise queue — each incoming action is enqueued as a thunk and executed only after the prior thunk resolves. This prevents race conditions without requiring explicit locks, which is crucial in Node.js where async handlers can interleave unpredictably.

tour.title: Player Actions & Settlement
tour.description: When a player sends fold/call/raise, DealerActionOrchestrator (apps/server/src/engine/dealer/orchestration/DealerActionOrchestrator.ts) receives it, deduplicates it via a per-hand idempotency key, dispatches to ActionOptionsService to validate the move, and then applies it through ActionService. After each action, SettlementService enforces strict chip conservation: blind debits, pot credits, split-pot payouts, and hand persistence to the database all happen atomically.

tour.title: Tournament System
tour.description: TournamentDirector (apps/server/src/tournaments/TournamentDirector.ts) runs on a periodic server tick and drives the full tournament lifecycle: processing scheduled starts, managing late registration windows, and seating players. When a hand ends at a tournament table, TournamentTableReconciler detects bust-outs, redistributes chips, and calls tournament-payouts.ts to calculate prize distribution based on field size. tournament-schedule.ts provides pure timing predicates (is late registration open? can a player rebuy?) used by both client and server.
tour.languageLesson: Tournament logic is split into pure functions (tournament-schedule.ts, tournament-payouts.ts) and stateful orchestrators (TournamentDirector). The pure functions are imported by both server and client, making them trivially unit-testable and preventing duplication of scheduling rules.

tour.title: Client State: Zustand Stores
tour.description: The client manages live game data through two complementary Zustand stores: table.store.ts holds the PokerState snapshot stream for a single active table, and multitable.store.ts manages sessions across multiple concurrent tables. The lobby.store.ts and tournaments.store.ts handle the pre-game listing screens. When a Colyseus state patch arrives over WebSocket, the table store absorbs it; all React components subscribe to store slices and re-render reactively without the server needing to push individual field updates.
tour.languageLesson: Zustand stores use a selector pattern: `useStore(state => state.someSlice)` means a component only re-renders when its specific slice changes. This is critical for a live poker table where the server sends 10+ state patches per hand — components that only care about pot size won't re-render on every seat-status update.

tour.title: The Table Adapter: Server State to View Models
tour.description: table.adapter.ts (apps/client/src/features/table/components/table/table.adapter.ts) is the translation layer with 15 fan-in imports — the highest in the client. It transforms raw PokerState snapshots from the server into strongly-typed view models the UI can render: it resolves the hero seat, maps opponents to their display slots, decodes encrypted hole cards, and formats chip amounts. This adapter pattern keeps the UI components free of any knowledge of the server's wire format.
tour.languageLesson: The adapter pattern decouples the server contract from the UI contract. Here, PokerState (Colyseus schema) flows in and a plain TypeScript view model flows out. When the server schema changes, only the adapter needs updating — not every component that renders seat or pot data.

tour.title: The Table UI: ActiveTableView & ActionBar
tour.description: ActiveTableView (apps/client/src/features/table/components/table/views/ActiveTableView.tsx) is the top-level React Native component that composes the full live poker table: opponent strip, hero zone, board cards, turn countdown, and the ActionBar. The ActionBar (ActionBar.tsx + actionBar.logic.ts) is architecturally notable because its wager calculation, permission derivation, and raise-amount logic are extracted into actionBar.logic.ts — a pure module with zero React imports — making it independently testable and reusable.

tour.title: Lobby Screen & Tournament Cards
tour.description: The lobby.tsx Expo Router screen (apps/client/app/lobby.tsx) is the player's entry point: it shows cash-game table listings, tournament cards, instant-start creation, and handles join/register flows. It polls for updates and subscribes to the lobby and tournament Zustand stores. This screen demonstrates the full client data flow in miniature: store subscription → Colyseus WebSocket events → re-render — the same pattern used throughout the app.

tour.title: Infrastructure: Docker & CI/CD
tour.description: The docker-compose.yml spins up a MySQL 8.4 database for local development, the only external service the project requires. On the CI side, contract-first.yml enforces that openapi.json is updated whenever openapi.ts changes (requiring a BREAKING marker for incompatible changes), while server-phase4-soak-gate.yml runs a 30-minute PokerRoom soak test on every engine or room change. These pipelines encode the team's quality gates: the contract-first check prevents silent API drift, and the soak gate catches concurrency bugs that unit tests miss.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use path-based triggers (`on.push.paths`) to run expensive tests only when relevant files change. The soak gate's 30-minute timeout is intentional: poker-room concurrency bugs (stalled turns, phantom hands) often only manifest after hundreds of consecutive hands under load.
